section_summary: This section consists chiefly of letters and petitions from American clergy, educators, missionaries, legislators, and private citizens urging the Roosevelt administration to stop exports of arms, aircraft, oil, metals, scrap iron, and other materials sustaining Japan’s war in China. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could be invoked only through a presidential finding of a state of war, would apply equally to China and Japan, and supplied no authority to embargo ordinary commodities; several replies also cite licensed arms exports and the Department’s condemnation of aerial bombing of civilians. The section also contains a continuation of an anti-Japanese-policy article, a cross-reference sheet, extensive petition signatures, and correspondence concerning Spain, China’s ports, the Munich settlement, and later American representations to Japan.

subfiles.title: Article advocating an end to American material support for Japan (continuation)
subfiles.about: The article argues that the United States should aid China and cease supplying Japan with materials used in its war.
subfiles.summary: The writer contends that Japan has become weakened and dependent on American supplies while conducting a brutal war that threatens both China and eventual American interests. Proposed measures include civilian relief, consumer boycotts, reprisals through selective export restrictions, and unofficial credits for China. The article concludes that the United States must stop acting, even indirectly, as provisioner of the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: Dwight Wilson Weist to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Weist forwards a copy of his letter to Senator George W. Norris concerning American war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Weist asks Roosevelt to note the enclosed copy of his appeal to Senator Norris. He says Norris was selected because he would be likely to understand the righteousness of the proposal.

subfiles.title: Dwight Wilson Weist to Senator George W. Norris
subfiles.about: Weist urges a congressional inquiry and application of neutrality legislation to the China-Japan conflict.
subfiles.summary: Weist reports claims that American citizens and businesses are prolonging Japan’s war against China by furnishing war materials. Rejecting the argument that other nations would supply Japan instead, he stresses American moral responsibility. He asks Congress and the Senate to determine whether a state of war exists and, if so, apply the neutrality statutes.

subfiles.title: John C. Hawk to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hawk condemns American supplies to Japan and urges Hull to lead efforts to end this material participation in the war.
subfiles.summary: Writing aboard the S.S. Empress of Japan while returning to China, Hawk recalls his recent meeting with Hull and describes shame that the United States supplies Japan with much of its war matériel. He invokes the atrocities at Nanking, Japanese violations of treaties and the Open Door, and the example of Korea and Manchukuo. Although opposed to war, he argues that Americans should be free to refuse sales to Japan and expresses hope that Hull will lead public action.

subfiles.title: Department of State forwarding letter for John C. Hawk
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Shanghai
subfiles.about: The Department transmits a letter for discretionary delivery to Reverend John C. Hawk.
subfiles.summary: The short official communication encloses a letter addressed to Reverend John C. Hawk. The consular officer in Shanghai is asked to deliver it at his discretion.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull to John C. Hawk
subfiles.about: Hull thanks Hawk, disclaims political ambitions, and sends material addressing the issues Hawk raised.
subfiles.summary: Hull recalls Hawk’s July visit and thanks him for his letter and generous personal comments. He states that he has no present or prospective personal political plans and is concentrating on foreign affairs. Enclosures include a statement, material on the international traffic in arms, and the Joint Resolution of May 1, 1937.

subfiles.title: Raymond Allston to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Allston asks how citizens and Christian groups can help stop American commercial support for Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Allston says the pamphlet “America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt” impressed him with the breadth of opposition to American corporations supplying Japan. He asks how citizens can make that sentiment effective and halt the traffic in instruments of death. He further argues that such conduct by professedly Christian nations undermines Chinese confidence in Christianity.
keywords: America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Raymond Allston
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the Neutrality Act’s limits and its decision not to proclaim a state of war between China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan, but that the President considers invocation contrary to American interests. He reports licensed arms exports since July 1937 of approximately $13.8 million to China and $10.63 million to Japan. The Act does not cover ordinary commodities, while the Secretary has publicly condemned civilian bombing and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: Bishop James Chamberlain Baker to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Baker asks Roosevelt to end the traffic sustaining Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Baker describes American trade as furnishing the sinews of Japan’s war. He urges the President to use every available power to end the traffic and says the hundreds of churches connected with him would support that position.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Bishop Baker
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department outlines the legal and policy reasons for not embargoing Japan under the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The response explains that a finding of war would require an embargo against both belligerents, and that the President considers invocation inconsistent with the country’s broader interests. It gives figures for licensed arms exports to China and Japan and notes that ordinary commodities cannot be restricted under the Act. A Joint Resolution and arms-traffic pamphlet are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Paul H. Maloney to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Maloney forwards a constituent’s postcard opposing supplies to Japan and requests the Department’s advice.
subfiles.summary: Representative Maloney transmits a postcard from Herman Borne of New Orleans. He asks Hull to consider and advise upon Borne’s appeal to stop American munitions, aircraft, scrap iron, and other supplies from reaching Japan.

subfiles.title: Herman Borne to Paul H. Maloney
subfiles.about: Borne urges Maloney to stop American war and industrial supplies from sustaining the slaughter in Asia.
subfiles.summary: Borne disclaims undue sympathy for either side but argues that American self-respect and Christian conscience require stopping the flow of munitions, planes, and scrap iron to Japan. He says employment and business should not be maintained at the cost of human blood and that Americans share responsibility if wars depend upon their supplies.

subfiles.title: Department of State to Paul H. Maloney
subfiles.about: The Department supplies a proposed explanation of neutrality law for Maloney to send to Herman Borne.
subfiles.summary: The Department recommends forwarding Borne copies of the Joint Resolution and arms-traffic pamphlet. Its proposed response explains that a presidential war proclamation would stop arms exports to both China and Japan, whereas no authority exists to single out Japan or restrict commodities outside the statutory arms list. It also supplies comparative figures for licensed arms exports and returns Borne’s postcard.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on the Nagasaki munitions industry
subfiles.from: State Department, Far Eastern Division (L. Bruner)
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects readers to a memorandum on munitions production and military stores in the Nagasaki Consular District.
subfiles.summary: This document-file note refers to file 894.20/216 and a State Department memorandum dated July 17, 1937. The referenced subject is the development of munitions industries and accumulation of military and naval stores in the Nagasaki Consular District for national-defense mobilization.

subfiles.title: J. E. Shoemaker to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Shoemaker forwards Madame Chiang Kai-shek’s appeal and urges firm international action, including withholding war materials from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Shoemaker quotes a June 4 letter from Madame Chiang thanking him for sympathy and expressing hope that benevolent governments will pressure Japan. Drawing on forty years as a missionary in China, he describes Japan’s attacks on civilians and argues that American and British war materials sustain the aggression. He proposes a firm but peaceful stand by law-abiding nations and asks Hull to find a course that will hasten the end of destruction in China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to J. E. Shoemaker
subfiles.about: Yost explains why the administration has not invoked the Neutrality Act and cites its condemnation of civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a war proclamation would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan and that the President has decided invocation would not serve the national interest. He cites licensed arms exports of roughly $13.8 million to China and $10.63 million to Japan and explains that non-arms commodities fall outside the Act. He also repeats Hull’s warning to bombing-plane manufacturers against materially encouraging attacks on civilians.

subfiles.title: Wisconsin missionary society appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Wisconsin State Convention of the Woman’s Missionary Society of the Evangelical Church
subfiles.about: Members of a Wisconsin women’s missionary convention petition Roosevelt to prohibit American war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The signers condemn the bombing of Chinese civilians and oppose shipments of gasoline, munitions, and raw materials to Japan. They ask Roosevelt to restrain industrial manufacturers and prohibit sales of war supplies. Four additional pages contain signatures and Wisconsin addresses, with one signer residing in Changsha, China.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Mrs. George Wickell
subfiles.about: Yost answers the Wisconsin missionary petition with the Department’s standard explanation of neutrality law and export policy.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that invoking the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that the President has determined this would not serve the national interest. It supplies arms-license totals for both countries and notes that the statute cannot restrict ordinary commodities. Yost also reiterates the government’s condemnation of bombing civilians and its warning to aircraft manufacturers.

subfiles.title: George W. Hinman to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hinman urges an embargo on steel, oil, copper, and scrap iron and stronger diplomatic opposition to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Recently returned from China, Hinman contrasts widespread American opposition to Japanese aggression with continued corporate sales of strategic materials. He argues that the government should regulate such exports, both as a moral duty and as part of the Good Neighbor policy. He calls for diplomatic pressure backed by a positive embargo on supplies essential to Japan’s war effort.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to George W. Hinman
subfiles.about: Yost explains that existing law does not authorize an embargo on scrap iron, steel, copper, or oil.
subfiles.summary: Yost outlines the Neutrality Act and the President’s decision not to invoke it because an arms embargo would apply equally to China and Japan. He gives comparative licensed-arms figures and stresses that scrap iron, steel, copper, and oil are absent from the statutory list. The reply closes by repeating the government’s condemnation of aerial bombing of civilians.

subfiles.title: John H. Cowles to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Cowles urges an end to munitions supplies for Japan while advocating removal of the arms embargo on Republican Spain.
subfiles.summary: Cowles writes as an individual citizen concerned about events in Europe and Asia. He asks the government to stop war munitions from reaching Japan during its invasion of China and to permit Spain’s loyalist government to obtain supplies against the insurgents.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore to John H. Cowles
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Moore explains the different statutory bases of the Spanish embargo and the administration’s policy toward China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moore states that lifting the Spanish embargo would require congressional repeal or a presidential finding that Spain’s civil strife had ended. Turning to East Asia, he explains that a finding of war would impose an arms embargo on both China and Japan, which the President believes contrary to American interests. He also notes that ordinary commodities cannot be embargoed and provides licensed-arms export figures for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Petition to the President on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.doc_type: petition with signature and form pages
subfiles.from: O. R. Tarwater and other petitioners
subfiles.about: The petition asks Roosevelt to end American trade and finance supporting Japan’s invasion and supports workers and businesses refusing such traffic.
subfiles.summary: The petition cites Japan’s violations of the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact, attacks on undefended cities, and use of American aircraft, bombs, shells, oil, trucks, and scrap iron. Its signers express solidarity with seamen, longshoremen, labor groups, financiers, and businesses refusing to assist Japan. Pages 227–228 contain further signatures, while pages 229–231 are additional petition or suggested-form sheets bearing the petition title.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to O. R. Tarwater
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the petition and explains the administration’s legal position on exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Tarwater and the other signers for transmitting their petition to the President. He explains that the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan only after a presidential finding of war, which the President has declined to make on national-interest grounds. The letter also cites export-license totals, the exclusion of ordinary commodities, and Hull’s condemnation of civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: Henry Huizinga to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Huizinga asks Roosevelt to stop American oil, metals, vehicles, and munitions from enabling Japanese bombing in China.
subfiles.summary: Huizinga describes daily reports of Chinese civilians killed by Japanese bombs and American exports that fuel aircraft or become weapons. He argues that Japanese gold payments bring little benefit while making Americans complicit in the violence. He endorses the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression and asks the President to stop the trade.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Henry Huizinga
subfiles.about: Yost explains the legal limitations on an embargo and the Department’s action against material encouragement of civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Yost repeats that invocation of the Neutrality Act would stop arms exports to both China and Japan and that the President has judged such action contrary to national interests. He supplies comparative arms-license totals and notes that the statute does not cover other commodities. He adds that the government has condemned civilian bombing and directly communicated that position to American aircraft and aeronautical-equipment firms.

subfiles.title: Frances K. Bement to Eleanor Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Bement invokes her work in China to ask how the United States can continue supplying Japan with materials used to kill civilians.
subfiles.summary: Bement describes devoting thirty-three years to children and women through a small hospital, a girls’ school, kindergarten, high school, and adult classes in China. She is distressed by reports that American war materials prolong the conflict and asks why concern for Japanese feelings should outweigh the lives of thousands. She closes by noting her enjoyment of Mrs. Roosevelt’s talks to the Chautauqua women’s club.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Frances K. Bement
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges Bement’s appeal and explains why the Department has not invoked the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: At Eleanor Roosevelt’s request, Yost thanks Bement for her letter and favorable comments about Mrs. Roosevelt’s talks. He explains that a presidential finding of war would stop arms exports to both China and Japan and that the administration regards invocation as contrary to American interests. He also gives licensed-arms figures and expresses hope that the Department’s position is clear.

subfiles.title: T. S. Wilder to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Wilder protests American supplies and credit to Japan and asks for public statements explaining current Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: Wilder argues that greatly increased American exports of munitions, scrap iron, and other products prolong an indefensible war and endanger future relations with China. He protests the extension of credit to Japan and urges a firmer policy in defense of American interests and nationals. Acknowledging his pro-Chinese outlook and limited knowledge of diplomacy, he requests relevant public reports or policy statements.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to T. S. Wilder
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains the absence of authority to restrict arms or credit selectively to Japan without invoking the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a presidential finding of war would prohibit both arms exports and credits to China and Japan, whereas no authority exists to restrict only Japan. The President has concluded that invocation would not serve broad American interests. The reply also cites arms-license totals and explains that commodities beyond the statutory arms list cannot be prohibited.

subfiles.title: E. C. Peters to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Peters urges Roosevelt to lead efforts in the next Congress to halt trade in war materials with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Peters joins other Christian citizens petitioning against continued American trade in war materials with Japan. While recognizing the executive difficulties, he asks Roosevelt to recommend practical legislative action at the next session of Congress.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore to E. C. Peters
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Moore acknowledges Peters’s views and gives the Department’s standard explanation of neutrality legislation and exports.
subfiles.summary: Moore assures Peters that his views will receive consideration and encloses the May 1, 1937 Joint Resolution. He explains that an arms embargo would follow only from a presidential finding of war and would apply to both China and Japan, a step the President considers contrary to American interests. The reply cites licensed-arms totals and notes that ordinary commodities are outside the Act.

subfiles.title: E. C. Peters to Cordell Hull on post-Munich policy
subfiles.about: Peters praises Hull’s post-Munich statements and hopes for more effective action against shipments of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Peters approves Hull’s recent foreign-policy statements and again asks for measures preventing war supplies from reaching Japan. He suggests that, because Japanese forces control China’s usable ports, application of the Neutrality Act might now burden Japan more heavily. He praises the Department’s September note to Japan and awaits the Japanese reply and any further American response.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore to E. C. Peters
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Moore thanks Peters for supporting administration policy and refers him to the Department’s earlier explanation.
subfiles.summary: Moore acknowledges Peters’s November letter and appreciates his favorable comments on the administration’s foreign policy. On preventing war-material shipments to Japan, he directs Peters to the Department’s letter and enclosures of September 8.

subfiles.title: George E. Bevans to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Bevans appeals for an embargo on American oil, iron, copper, and military equipment destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bevans expresses sorrow that American suppliers are helping Japan wage an aggressive war and kill Chinese civilians. Claiming the United States supplies more oil, iron, copper, and war equipment than all other countries combined, he asks Hull to find a means of stopping the shipments.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to George E. Bevans
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains that oil, iron, and copper lie outside the Neutrality Act and cannot be embargoed under existing law.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential finding of war would embargo arms to both China and Japan, but that the President has decided against invocation on national-interest grounds. He supplies arms-license totals for the two countries. Because oil, iron, and copper are not classed as arms, no existing statute authorizes the President or Secretary of State to prohibit their export.

subfiles.title: George Holden Tinkham to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Tinkham forwards a constituent’s questions about executive authority and public identification of exporters supplying Japan.
subfiles.summary: Tinkham quotes a constituent asking whether the government can prohibit all war-material exports to Japan without congressional consent. The constituent also proposes that the State Department request voluntary cessation, as with bombing planes, and publicize the names of firms that disregard the request.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore to George Holden Tinkham
subfiles.about: Moore answers that exports cannot generally be forbidden without statutory authority and that advisory requests are reserved for exceptional cases such as civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Moore states that arms exports can be prohibited only following a presidential proclamation under the Neutrality Act, while the government has no statutory authority over other commodities. He explains that the aircraft request rested on the United States’ categorical condemnation of aerial attacks on civilian populations. The Department undertakes advisory action of that kind only in exceptional circumstances.
